<reason>Both sides argued cleanly and stayed largely within the evidence rules, but B built the more coherent path to victory. B's calendar attack forced A to concede in Rebuttal 2 that new-build contributes "close to zero" in-window generation — effectively conceding half of the literal motion. B then hit the core of A's remaining case (life-extension = "reduce") with the "stale counterfactual" argument: since retiring reactors are increasingly backfilled by clean renewables rather than gas, the avoided-emissions story behind extension shrinks toward zero, while renewables' avoided tons are measured against fossil plants running today, with no hypothetical required. A never squarely rebutted this until the final closing, where A pivoted to a portfolio/"freeing renewable dollars" framing — a clever move, but one that implicitly concedes extension itself isn't the reducer, just an enabler. B's closing seized exactly on that concession ("extension makes the renewable dollar count... that is not the faster reducer"), landing the last and most damaging blow of the debate, one A had no opportunity to answer. Pressure-question compliance was strong on both sides (clear Q1/Q2 and A1/A2 formatting), but B's answers more directly neutralized the tension A exposed, while A's late reframe read as a new line introduced in closing rather than a crystallization of existing clash.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's "stale counterfactual" argument (B2.2/B4.1) — that clean backfill increasingly nullifies extension's avoided-emissions claim — combined with B's closing punch that A's own portfolio reframe concedes nuclear is an "enabler" rather than a "reducer," which A never got to rebut.</best_rebuttal>
